children: Oil markets are learning to live with a strange new reality in the
: no war, no peace, and plenty of danger in between.

Oil prices have settled into a $90-$95 a barrel range in recent days after tumbling more than 20% since the start of the month. That does not mean things are calm on the ground, however. Far from it. Iran has intensified attacks on tankers around the Strait of Hormuz and struck targets in Bahrain and Kuwait, while US forces have hit Iranian military targets.

But for now, markets are nervously waiting for President Donald Trump’s next move: attack, strike a quick peace deal, or maintain the status quo, the blockade on Iran’s oil exports, in hopes that Tehran eventually concedes defeat.

Nearly nine months into the Iran war, the International Energy Agency says the conflict has permanently reshaped the global energy system. The biggest disruption to global oil and gas trade in recorded history could ultimately accelerate the shift away from fossil fuels, with world oil demand potentially more than 4% lower by 2035 than previous estimates if governments step up electrification, efficiency and fuel switching, the IEA said in a report.
Meanwhile, the world’s attention shifted this week to Shenzhen in southern China, where Trump and his Chinese and Russian counterparts Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin held
on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, with energy security among the issues on the table.

One major power was conspicuous in its absence: Europe. The world’s largest trade bloc had no seat at the table, underscoring the widening gap between Europe’s enormous economic weight and its limited geopolitical clout.
For more on that, read my column.
In other news:
China’s independent refiners are feeling the Iran squeeze and responding accordingly.
Saudi Arabia is clawing back market share in India.

Ukraine’s campaign targeting Russia’s refineries is biting hard. Drone attacks have slashed Russian refineries’ combined crude processing volumes by 45% since late October, according to estimates from two industry sources.
China is stockpiling oil again. ROI Asia Commodities Columnist Clyde Russell breaks down what’s happening.

America’s energy export boom may be entering a tougher phase. ROI Energy Transition Columnist Gavin Maguire explains why the dramatic market-share gains that helped make the US an energy superpower will be increasingly difficult to repeat.
